content: In the United Kingdom, individuals aged 17 to 21 years represent 7% of all licensed drivers but account for 13% of drivers involved in road traffic crashes that result in injuries. To address this issue, the UK government, like many others, has proposed implementing driver education programs in schools and colleges. However, there is concern that such programs might lead to earlier licensing, which could inadvertently increase the number of teenagers involved in road traffic crashes. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of school-based driver education on both the likelihood of obtaining a driving license and the involvement in road traffic crashes. To achieve this, researchers conducted a systematic search of databases, including CENTRAL, CIG's specialized register, MEDLINE, the National Research Register, and the Science & Social Science Citation Index. They also reviewed reference lists of relevant studies and contacted authors and experts in the field. The study included randomized controlled trials that compared school-based driver education to no driver education, specifically assessing the effects on licensing rates and road traffic crash involvement. Two independent authors screened the search results, extracted data, and assessed the quality of the trials. Three trials conducted between 1982 and 1984 met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 17,965 participants. Two of these trials examined the effect of driver education on licensing rates. In a trial conducted by Stock in the United States, 87% of students who received driver education obtained their driving license, compared to 84.3% in the control group (relative risk [RR] 1.04; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02 to 1.05). In another trial by Wynne-Jones in New Zealand, the time from enrollment in the trial to obtaining a license was significantly shorter for those who received driver education. Specifically, males in the driver education group obtained their licenses in 111 days on average, compared to 300 days for males in the control group. Similarly, females in the driver education group obtained their licenses in 105 days on average, compared to 415 days for females in the control group. All three trials also assessed the effect of driver education on road traffic crashes. In a trial conducted by Strang in Australia, 42% of students in both the driver education and control groups experienced one or more crashes after obtaining their licenses (RR 1.01; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.23). In the trial by Stock, 27.5% of students in the driver education group were involved in one or more crashes as drivers, compared to 26.7% in the control group (RR 1.03; 95% CI 0.98 to 1.09). In the trial by Wynne-Jones, 16% of students in the driver education group experienced crashes, compared to 14.5% in the control group (RR 1.10; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.59). The authors concluded that school-based driver education programs lead to earlier licensing among teenagers. However, there is no evidence to suggest that these programs reduce the likelihood of involvement in road traffic crashes. On the contrary, the findings indicate that driver education may result in a modest but potentially significant increase in the proportion of teenagers involved in traffic crashes.
